strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap in differential privacy accounting: tight, efficient PLD-based accounting for random allocation / k-out-of-t sampling, a scheme with practical relevance for DP-SGD and communication-efficient private aggregation.

The main technical contribution is substantial. The PLD-realization formalism, direct PLD transformations for Poisson subsampling, and the random-allocation computation via convolutions of exponentiated PLDs are useful conceptual and algorithmic tools beyond a narrow special case.

The theoretical claims are generally well supported: the manuscript gives formal reductions, validity/tightness guarantees, runtime bounds, and detailed proofs in the appendices. The distinction between stochastic domination and hockey-stick domination is handled carefully.

The numerical evaluation is convincing for the motivating Gaussian setting: the proposed method improves over prior analytical/RDP bounds, nearly matches lower bounds where available, and includes runtime scaling, comparisons to Monte Carlo estimates, k>1 settings, and a PREAMBLE accounting case study.
The paper is well situated in the literature and clearly explains why existing Poisson, shuffle, Monte Carlo, epsilon-delta, and RDP accounting approaches are insufficient for the targeted workflows.
weaknesses: The strongest application-facing claim, that random allocation is better suited for DP-SGD, is only indirectly supported. The paper relies mostly on prior utility results plus privacy accounting and includes only a toy privacy-utility experiment, not end-to-end DP-SGD training experiments under the new accountant.

Reproducibility is only partially adequate. The manuscript mentions an implementation, but the citation appears incomplete and the experimental setup lacks enough detail to fully reproduce all numerical plots, especially the PREAMBLE results using 10^6 bins, numerical precision choices, and cluster/laptop hardware differences.

The evaluation is heavily centered on Gaussian mechanisms. The method is advertised as general for arbitrary PLD realizations and arbitrary noise distributions, but there is little empirical evidence for non-Gaussian mechanisms or more heterogeneous accounting pipelines.

For k>1 random allocation, the approach depends on a known lossy reduction to composition of 1-out-of-floor(t/k) allocation. The paper acknowledges rounding/suboptimality, but the practical impact and possible alternatives are not deeply explored.

The manuscript lacks a dedicated limitations and broader-impact/ethics discussion. This is not a major ethical concern because the work improves privacy accounting, but limitations around numerical stability, extreme delta regimes, implementation complexity, and possible misuse of overly optimistic accounting should be stated more explicitly.

Presentation is dense and notation-heavy, with several places where the add/remove direction notation and algorithm descriptions are hard to parse. The paper is readable for DP-accounting experts but may be difficult for a broader ICML audience to use without clearer pseudocode-to-implementation guidance.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically relevant gap in differential privacy accounting: tight PLD-based accounting for random allocation/k-out-of-t sampling, which has direct motivation from DP-SGD implementations and communication-constrained private aggregation.
weaknesses: The empirical section is narrower than the claims suggest. Most numerical evidence is for Gaussian mechanisms and privacy-accounting curves, while the broader claims about random allocation being a better practical alternative to Poisson sampling rely heavily on prior utility results plus a toy experiment rather than new end-to-end DP-SGD evidence.

strengths: The paper makes a technically meaningful contribution: it derives a PLD-based accounting method for 1-out-of-t random allocation, extends it to k-out-of-t via an existing reduction, and connects this to general PLD realization operations including Poisson subsampling. This is a useful advance over prior hockey-stick/RDP analyses because PLDs compose accurately and integrate with existing accounting workflows.

The theoretical development is mostly convincing. The central identity expressing the random-allocation PLD through convolutions of exponentiated PLDs is elegant, and the stochastic-domination/discretization analysis gives a clear validity and tightness story with explicit alpha/beta approximation parameters and runtime bounds.

The numerical evaluation is well aligned with the claims: comparisons against prior analytic bounds, Monte Carlo estimates, Poisson subsampling, runtime scaling, k>1 behavior, and the PREAMBLE accounting example collectively show that the method can materially improve practical privacy accounting in relevant regimes.

The contribution is significant for private ML systems because random allocation/balls-and-bins style sampling is closer to practical batching and communication constraints than idealized Poisson sampling, yet has lacked tight usable accounting. The paper also broadens PLD accounting beyond pure composition in a way that others could build on.

The manuscript is generally well organized, with clear motivation, explicit algorithms in the appendix, and an honest discussion of numerical stability, FFT tradeoffs, lossy k reduction, and regimes where Poisson and random allocation are incomparable.
weaknesses: Some headline claims are slightly broader than the evidence supports. For example, the paper says the results establish random allocation as a better and more practical alternative to Poisson subsampling, but the privacy comparison is not uniform, the utility argument mostly relies on prior work plus a toy experiment, and the strongest empirical case is centered on Gaussian mechanisms and selected DP-SGD/PREAMBLE settings.

Reproducibility is adequate but not ideal. The paper mentions an implementation, but the reference is incomplete in the manuscript text, and several numerical details needed to exactly reproduce all figures are scattered or partial. The PREAMBLE experiment uses 10^6 bins and appears computationally heavy, but runtime/memory requirements and exact implementation settings are not fully specified.

The k>1 result inherits a lossy reduction to repeated 1-out-of-floor(t/k) allocation. The paper acknowledges this, but for regimes where the rounding loss is non-negligible the practical tightness and comparison to alternatives remain less settled.

The presentation is dense and assumes substantial familiarity with PLD accounting, stochastic domination, and DP amplification. The main paper sometimes compresses important proof intuition into appendices, and a few notation/wording issues and typos reduce readability.

The limitations and ethics discussion are relatively lightweight. The work is privacy-enhancing, so ethical risks are not central, but deployment caveats around numerical precision, parameter misuse, and over-interpreting privacy improvements in full training pipelines could be made more explicit.
